items.problem: “Tracked … rock and how often studies report” hides the multiplication and could mean any loose relationship. C59 tests rates proportional to the product in each time interval. “How often” also obscures that the measure is a share of studies. “Almost no” is faithful; omitting “post hoc” and 0.1 is acceptable here because the sentence clearly reports the model’s failure.
items.suggested_fix: If finding rates changed in proportion to North American rock area (for rocks formed outside the sea) multiplied by the share of studies reporting trilete spores, the early absence would fit those ancestors even with all 48 finds independent. But this model predicts almost no late-Silurian finds, where at least 13 occur.

items.problem: “Together” hides multiplication, and “rock” loses the area measure. “Fell enough before” obscures a comparison of averages before and after the oldest find. “Every count” should mean every tested count; “same amount” should mean the same relative change. “Followed them closely” overstates the rejection: the test contradicts proportional changes in each interval, not every close relationship. The immediate appearance of recognisable bodies correctly conveys zero delay.
items.suggested_fix: Multiplying North American rock area (for rocks formed outside the sea) by the share of studies reporting three-rayed spores gives a measure whose average was much lower before the oldest find than after it. Ancestors at 444–452 Ma fit all four tested counts of independent finds, even if recognisable bodies appeared immediately, provided average finding rates were lower by the same factor. But rates proportional to this product in each time interval would predict almost no late-Silurian finds, where at least 13 occur. Using the difference between the earlier and later averages therefore requires a separate assumption that average finding rates differed by the same factor.
